sources.title: Active Data Lakes: Regaining Physical Data Independence Without Losing Interoperability
sources.publication_date_evidence: Official Volume 19 No.6 front matter says February 2026; paper front page establishes volume/pages/DOI. Exact first-online date not verified. Search aggregators supplied conflicting dates and were not used.
sources.venue: PVLDB 19(6):1372–1385; VLDB 2026 Research 44, Lakehouse and Open Table Formats
sources.read_scope: Full 14-page final publication PDF extracted locally; main text §§1–8.4 read. Page 1378 Figure 5 and experimental setup visually rendered and checked. References inspected for context, not treated as additional independently read sources.
mechanisms: Active service virtualizes the on-wire Parquet interface over a different physical format (BtrBlocks), preserving legacy Parquet range readers.
Footer and range offsets must be predictable before conversion; the prototype forgoes general-purpose compression and retains suitable dictionary/bit-packed encodings.
The article focuses on the file-virtualization experiment. Separate prefetching and trickling-insert prototypes were read but their results are deliberately not combined.

performance_scope.hosts: Separate AWS c5n.9xlarge machines for DuckDB and HTTP service, same availability zone; paper reports 50 Gib/s network
performance_scope.comparison: Virtualized Parquet over BtrBlocks versus Zstd-compressed native Parquet

limitations: Author measurements, not independently reproduced.
No generalized end-to-end benchmark claim for all Iceberg/Paimon workloads. Paimon was not evaluated.
Additional active service and greater wire volume must be budgeted.
§8.4 states optimizations were evaluated separately and a distributed implementation addressing scalability and availability remains future work.
access_gaps: Web PDF open failed with Internal Error; exact official PDF downloaded successfully over HTTPS and all pages were available locally.
No prototype execution or failure testing was performed.

sources.title: The Streamhouse And Lakestream With Apache Fluss
sources.author_affiliation: Both identified on article as Fluss PMC members
sources.read_scope: All article sections, including read/write scope and responsibility boundaries; relevant fragment IDs verified against HTML.
mechanisms: One logical table coordinates lake snapshots and stream progress; supported union readers must respect table semantics rather than concatenate all rows.
Open lake-file compatibility is insufficient for a union reader; managed writes and schema changes need supported coordination.
Reusable table storage does not replace transformation engines, specialized indexes or all transactional requirements.

performance_scope.note: Architecture argument; no measured end-to-end speedup or universal copy-elimination count. Publication is new, not necessarily every described capability.

limitations: No universal simultaneous snapshot across every engine and table.
Arbitrary independent writes to the lake layer are not promised.
Supported integration, table type and release determine behavior.

sources.title: Tiering Service Deep Dive Part 1: The Mental Model
sources.read_scope: Whole mechanism article, especially heartbeat, frozen stopping offsets and ordered commit reporting.
mechanisms: Planner freezes per-bucket stopping offsets; data files and corresponding progress belong to the lake commit.
After lake snapshot durability, lake offsets are recorded in Fluss metadata; task-completion heartbeat is triggered immediately.
New attempts carry new epochs so old completion reports can be ignored.

performance_scope.note: Worked walkthrough uses illustrative time/offset values. Draft uses its own explicitly labeled 100/140 example, not measured input.

limitations: Blog is a mechanism explanation, not a pinned-version code audit.
Do not turn the pedagogical state-machine labels into source-code enum names.

The June 4 sentence claiming lake lag always includes a full freshness interval is too broad; the June 9 timing explanation distinguishes best/worst arrival positions. Draft uses only the qualified June 9 timing model.

sources.title: Tiering Service Deep Dive Part 2: Tuning
sources.read_scope: Table kinds, scheduling/freshness, force-finish exception, multi-table reads/serialized commits, scaling-out qualifications.
mechanisms: Normal next-round eligibility is measured from completion, so start-to-start cadence includes the preceding round duration.
Log splits can force-finish, but an existing-KV-snapshot bootstrap must complete to establish the incremental offset.
Queue delay and serialized commits affect observable lake freshness beyond the configured interval.

performance_scope.illustrative_model: 5-minute freshness plus stable 90-second rounds gives approximately 6.5-minute start cadence and a record just missing cutoff can wait about 8 minutes.
assumptions: One table or no additional queue waiting
performance_scope.note: Timing illustration, not author benchmark or SLA.

limitations: PK startup without an existing KV snapshot instead uses log splits and has different force-finish behavior.
Do not apply the simple cadence model to multi-table backlog or first snapshot bootstrap.
access_gaps: No runtime metrics or independent performance reproduction.

sources.title: LESS is More for I/O-Efficient Repairs in Erasure-Coded Storage

publication_date.evidence: Official BibTeX month=feb, year=2026; PDF cover gives conference February 24–26.

public_by.evidence: Official session page says papers available to everyone beginning Tuesday, February 24. Earliest prepublication upload not established.

sources.read_scope: Original 12-page proceedings PDF: main text sections 1–5, MDS proof appendix and artifact appendix. Original PDF table 2 and figures 3–5 visually checked in cloud browser, printed pages 636–637.

claims.claim: Small configurable sub-packetization and overlapping extended RS sub-stripes permit single-block repair within one extended sub-stripe; MDS retained with suitable coefficients.
claims.support: §3.1–3.4, Figure 1, Theorem 1 and Appendix A.

claims.claim: For (n,k)=(14,10), LESS alpha=4 reads 4.64 blocks on average with 13 seeks; Clay alpha=256 reads 3.25 with 286 average seeks.
claims.support: Table 2, printed p.636; numerical analysis, not a throughput measurement.

claims.claim: LESS alpha=4 reduces default single-block repair time by 50.8% versus RS and 33.9% versus Clay.
claims.support: §4.2 Exp#B1 and Figure 4(a).

claims.claim: Single-thread 256 KiB packet encoding throughput: RS 2.8 GiB/s; LESS alpha=4 1.6 GiB/s.
claims.support: §4.2 Exp#B3 and Figure 4(c).

claims.claim: Full-node recovery experiment repairs 20 blocks from different stripes, one failed block per stripe.
claims.support: §4.2 Methodology, printed p.636.

benchmark_context.software: OpenEC atop Hadoop 3.3.4 HDFS; Jerasure coding; Ubuntu 22.04
benchmark_context.hardware: Each machine: quad-core Intel i5-7500 at 3.4 GHz, 16 GiB RAM, 7200 RPM 1 TB SATA HDD
benchmark_context.network: 10 Gbps Ethernet switch; default per-machine bandwidth limited to 1 Gbps with Wondershaper
benchmark_context.statistical_method: Mean of 10 runs; 95% confidence intervals using Student t distribution
benchmark_context.encoding_microbenchmark: One in-memory stripe with random bytes; single-thread throughput; distinct from disk/network repair

limitations: Controlled HDD cluster; no NVMe result is claimed.
20-block recovery is much smaller than a production full disk.
Encoding throughput penalty must be counted alongside repair benefit.
Efficient multi-block repair is conditional on failed blocks belonging to the same block group and sufficient sub-stripe redundancy; not a blanket faster arbitrary multi-failure claim.
No independently reproduced result in this task.
editorial_inference: Suggested foreground-tail-latency and full-capacity rebuild experiments are our engineering recommendations, not completed paper experiments.
gaps: No production-scale measurement supplied for full-capacity node rebuild.
